title: $NVDA: I Know What You Want to See — My Bottom
body:
A Madam 8 production 

🎧Drop it like its Hot - Snoop Dogg (feat Pharell ) 



Ooo. Weee.  

She’s just your type, isn’t she?

Nvidia is a technology company that makes special computer parts called GPUs (graphics processing units). 

Think of them like extremely fast brains for computers that can solve thousands of math problems at the same time.
—

💚So What . Its Nvidia💚

Originally, Nvidia made these GPUs so video games would look amazing — explosions, water, lighting, and characters moving smoothly across the screen.

But those same chips turned out to be perfect for artificial intelligence.

AI is essentially teaching computers to recognize patterns and solve problems in ways that resemble human thinking. 

That’s how things like ChatGPT writing stories, self-driving cars recognizing roads, computers analyzing X-rays, and robots learning tasks all work.

Nvidia doesn’t build the entire computer or phone. Instead, it designs these powerful chips, for huge companies like:
	•	Microsoft
	•	Alphabet (google)
	•	Amazon 
These household names buy billions of dollars worth of them to build massive AI data centers — giant computer rooms sometimes called AI factories.

————
💚Nvidia is cute. What does that have to do with me?💚

You probably use Nvidia technology without even realizing it.

	
👉Video games on PCs, PlayStations, or Xbox often rely on Nvidia graphics technology.

👉When you talk to AI assistants or chatbots, those answers are frequently generated on Nvidia chips inside large data centers.

👉Self-driving vehicles, movie special effects, medical imaging tools, and even weather forecasting models run faster thanks to Nvidia.
	
Even if you don’t buy the stock directly, Nvidia might still affect your finances.

Yes. You’re already in a Situationship.

If you own a retirement account, index fund, or ETF tracking the S&P 500, Nvidia is already inside it. 

As of March 2026, Nvidia represents roughly 7.8% of the SPY ETF, meaning its movements can significantly influence the overall market.

So if Nvidia catches a headache. Trust you might have a bad night.

———-
💚Nvidia has a pretty face but uhh💚

She’s a darling indeed.
She has risen like a queen and exceeded despite all odds

Her 5-year total return: +1,318% (roughly 13× your money).

Her 1-year return: +57%.

Even her YTD 2026 performance looks good: +2.5% (a slower start after huge prior gains).

When a stock runs as hard as Nvidia has, every investor eventually asks the same question.

Its Not:

“How high can she go?”

But quietly…
“Where’s the bottom?”

curiosity?  Or jealousy. Maybe it’s just human nature.

Just like a room full of gentlemen pretending they aren’t looking, traders watch Nvidia the same way people watch a beautiful woman walk into the room.

They’re polite.
They smile.
But eventually someone whispers:

“I wonder what that  bottom will looks like “ 

And in markets, that means something very specific.

It means:
Where might Nvidia actually fall when the beauty fades ?

Before we talk about those numbers, let’s talk about the signals traders look for before she turns around and shows it.
————
💚Are We Getting Close to tappin that💚

Experienced traders know bottoms rarely appear out of nowhere.

Charts are the athletic leisure wear.  TA can give you a glimpse of what may lie beneath. 


One of the tools many professionals watch is volume profile analysis.

Instead of focusing only on price, volume profile shows where the largest amount of shares historically traded. These zones reveal where institutional investors previously built positions.

For Nvidia, the biggest volume clusters from the AI rally appear around three major areas.


High Volume Nodes (Institutional Support)
	•	$155–160 — consolidation during the AI breakout
	•	$140–145 — major institutional accumulation zone
	•	$120–130 — deep historical support from earlier base building

These areas matter because large funds previously bought shares there. If the price revisits these levels, those same participants often step in again.

Traders call these zones support shelves.
If one shelf breaks, the stock often moves quickly to the next.

Level	Technical Meaning
$160	First support shelf
$145	AI rally accumulation
$125	Deep semiconductor cycle support


Markets rarely fall randomly.
 They usually travel between liquidity zones where large amounts of shares previously traded.

How All the Signals Combine
Traders begin preparing for a correction when several signals appear together:

	•	RSI divergence above 70
	•	Loss of the 50-day moving average (~$165–170)
	•	Multiple distribution days
	•	Semiconductor peers weakening
	•	Price approaching volume profile support zones
	•	
When these signals start clustering, technicians stop asking if the stock might pull back. 

Thats Nvidia getting up out of her seat and turning around . Lady phase is coming to an end . And her twerking, marks at the beginning of a new phase.


They start asking:


How far might it go?

Quick Technical Summary for NVDA


Indicator	Level Traders Watch
RSI Divergence	Above 70–75
50-day MA	~$165–170
Volume Profile Support	$160 / $145 / $125
200-day MA	~$125–135


But This Is Nvidia
She’s a lady.
Surely she wouldn’t do something like that.
Right?
______

💚Situations That Could Make Nvidia Show Her Bottom💚


Charts show when momentum weakens.
But the real reasons corrections happen usually come from outside the chart.
——-

💚The Classic Bear Case 💚

When analysts debate Nvidia’s downside risk, the same arguments appear:

	1.	Extreme valuation — the stock is priced for perfection
	2.	Hyperscalers building their own chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium)
	3.	AI demand normalizing after the initial infrastructure boom
	4.	Competition from AMD and custom silicon
	5.	Semiconductor cycles historically boom and bust

Those are well known.

But there’s another risk worth discussing.
———-
💚Sidepieces with a red flag: War💚

A prolonged conflict involving Iran could hurt Nvidia — but not necessarily because China stops buying chips.

The real issue would be energy and supply chains. 

Yep Nvidia is in a Situationship. She has side piece with big chip energy.

The Strait of Hormuz

The Strait of Hormuz carries about 20% of the world’s oil supply.

If conflict disrupted that route:
	•	oil prices could spike
	•	global shipping would slow
	•	inflation pressures would rise
That alone could push the global economy toward recession.
———

💚AI Data Centers Need Enormous Energy💚

AI infrastructure requires tremendous electricity.
If energy prices surge:

	•	data center expansion becomes more expensive
	•	AI infrastructure spending slows
	•	demand for Nvidia GPUs weakens

Semiconductor Manufacturing Depends on Global Resources

Chip manufacturing requires materials and energy from multiple regions.

Examples include:
	•	helium used in semiconductor fabrication
	•	electricity for chip factories
	•	shipping routes connecting global suppliers
If supply chains break, chip production slows everywhere.

Taiwan’s Energy Dependency
Most advanced Nvidia chips are manufactured by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ($TSM) 

Taiwan imports almost all its energy. If global energy supply becomes unstable, the cost of running semiconductor fabricators could increase dramatically.

💚The Real Macro Risk💚

A Hormuz disruption could trigger:
	•	oil prices above $120–150
	•	global inflation
	•	central bank tightening
	•	falling technology spending

In that environment:
	•	AI investment slows
	•	tech stocks correct
	•	Nvidia loses momentum ( bye bye SPY)

———
💚The Hidden Geopolitical Shock💚

But wait, there’s more

Some event analysts quietly watch something that has nothing to do with China or Iran.

Russia restricting exports of semiconductor materials.

Russia produces about 40% of the world’s palladium, while Ukrainian facilities historically supplied most semiconductor-grade neon gas.

These materials are critical for chip manufacturing.

If those supplies were disrupted:
	•	semiconductor production could slow
	•	chip shortages could reappear
	•	Nvidia and other chip companies could drop sharply

Markets already experienced a preview of this risk during the 2022 Russia-Ukraine invasion, when neon supplies collapsed.

A weak economy in America, may trigger Russia to pounce. 

OK, so let’s say the worst happens.

Nvidia flipped it on us and it’s no longer the lady we thought she was.

She backs it up and begins to show us her bottom.

💚What would that  Bottom look like?💚

Ooo. Yall so freaky

Traders often watch the following structure:

50-day moving average: ~ $165–170 First support zone: $160 Second support zone: $140–150
 200-day moving average: ~ $125–135 Deep correction zone: $120–130


Here is a simple hierarchy:

1️⃣ Lose the 50-day → momentum cooling 2️⃣ Lose the 200-day → major trend shift 3️⃣ Next support → $150 then $130

————

💚What Will You Do When You See It?💚
Seeing signals early doesn’t mean predicting the exact bottom.

So you have to be ready with a plan not just a camera for a pic. 

Knowing where Nvidia’s potential bottom may fall, gives traders, investors options.

Some investors, traders might:

	•take profits after extended runs -leave the relationship entirely.
	•wait for pullbacks before buying-think Nvidia is a high value girl and this is their time to y the number and move in.
	•sell options into volatility-hang around and clap cheeks 
	•scale into positions gradually- 

I currently don’t own Nvidia. She too pricey  

BUT 

if I saw her drop it REAL low, 

trust

 I would be tempted to get a
 credit card out and slide it right down the center. 

Anyhow 

The goal isn’t perfect predicted numbers.

The goal is not being surprised when she drops it low 
——-

💚The Final Thought💚

Don’t get me wrong. Im not a hater. 

Nvidia has been one of the most extraordinary runs in modern market history. A beautiful lady that is smart, has long-term potential for marriage.


When a lady moves that beautifully. 
Everyone eventually wonders the same thing.

“I bet you want to see that a$$.”

Yes it is cringe 

Just remember.
By the time everyone is staring…
the smart money has usually already left the table.

title: When will I learn? 2️⃣
body:
🎧Mistakes- Sharon Van Ettenn  🎧

2️⃣ Benjamin Graham 

In 1919, early in his career, Benjamin Graham—along with partners and friends—invested heavily (about $60,000, equivalent to over $1 million today) in Pennsylvania Savold Tire and related Savold Tire ventures.

These were speculative promotions exploiting a purported patented process for retreading automobile tires. Graham had earlier profited nicely from the original Savold Tire (initial $2,500 investment turned into quick gains), fueling greed and leading him to participate impulsively in the larger Pennsylvania deal without full due diligence.

The stocks initially hyped up (with flashy promotions like electric signs in Columbus Circle), but the scheme collapsed dramatically: trading halted, the parent stock plunged to 12½, and soon “no bid” was quoted for any Savold issues. All three related companies vanished from records as if they never existed—exposed as fraudulent promotions where funds were diverted by the promoter.

Graham salvaged only partial recovery (about 10–30% in some accounts via pressure on the promoter), resulting in a near-total wipeout of the $60,000. This painful early debacle, amid the post-WWI speculative frenzy, deeply influenced Graham: it reinforced the dangers of speculation, greed, and insufficient analysis, prompting him to develop his core principles of rigorous security analysis and the famous “margin of safety” to protect against such losses and over-optimism.

title: When will I learn? 1️⃣:  🍀 Irish I was lucky
body:
🎧Beautiful Mistakes- Maroon 5 and Megan Thee Stallion  🎧

Lets end this series big👀

1️⃣ Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway)

In 1993, Warren Buffett acquired Dexter Shoe Company—a Maine-based footwear manufacturer—for approximately $433 million, paid entirely with 25,203 shares of Berkshire Hathaway Class A stock (rather than cash).
He overestimated Dexter’s durable competitive advantage (“moat”), believing its U.S. manufacturing strength would endure. Instead, intense competition from low-cost imports (especially from China and Asia) quickly eroded its position: sales collapsed, production shifted offshore, U.S. operations ceased by 2001, and the business became essentially worthless (folded into H.H. Brown Shoe Group with minimal value).

The true devastation came from paying with Berkshire stock: those shares, had Buffett retained them, would today be worth billions (estimates range from $9–19 billion+ depending on the date and share price, reflecting Berkshire’s extraordinary long-term compounding). Buffett has repeatedly called this his worst single investment or “most gruesome mistake,” even joking it deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records as a financial disaster—primarily due to the massive opportunity cost to shareholders from diluting ownership in a compounding powerhouse to buy a failing one.

Key lesson he emphasized: Never pay with stock for a mediocre or vulnerable business, and rigorously assess true economic moats against global competition.

title: Its time to learn 8️⃣ : Ken Griffin
body:
Its time to learn 8️⃣ : Ken Griffin 

🎧Happy - Pharell. 🎧

8️⃣ Ken Griffin (Citadel)

Ken Griffin, the founder and CEO of Citadel, has built one of the most successful hedge funds in history, with Citadel often ranked as the most profitable ever 

We reviewed his worst mistake here👇

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bjoG/wheeeennnnnn-will-i-learn-8

Now , here  are some of the main things Ken Griffin got right in investing, based on his own reflections, Citadel’s performance, and analyses of the firm’s approach:

1.   Griffin started trading as a Harvard student in the late 1980s, focusing on convertible bonds. He identified that many were mispriced, built algorithms to find opportunities, and used a long convertible/short stock strategy to profit from volatility. This niche edge generated strong early returns (e.g., 43% in 1991, 40% in 1992) and laid the foundation for Citadel’s launch in 1990.

2. . Griffin embraced quant analytics aggressively, giving Citadel an advantage in data processing, modeling, and execution. This tech-forward mindset scaled across multi-strategy investing (equities, fixed income, commodities, derivatives) and helped navigate volatile markets consistently.

3.  Griffin repeatedly emphasizes defining a clear advantage before entering any space: “What can we do better or differently?” Without an identifiable edge there’s no point competing.

4.  From the start, he hired bright, ambitious young people (often paying above Wall Street rates), gave them real responsibility, and paired them with experienced experts.

5.  Citadel prioritizes capital preservation above all, with robust systems, centralized oversight, and a “pod” model where sector teams operate but under strict risk controls.

6.  Rather than top-down control, Citadel empowers world-class portfolio managers and teams closest to the information to make calls.

7.  Moved beyond single approaches to a multi-strategy platform (fundamental equities, quant, fixed income, etc.) reduced reliance on any one market or style, contributing to consistent outperformance even in tough years.

8. Griffin has advocated nimble, risk-neutral strategies that avoid crowded “safe” trades (e.g., rushing into gold or cash prematurely).

9.  He personally reviews P&L sheets daily and spends time analyzing successes (not just failures) to reinforce positive patterns.

10.  Griffin’s emphasis on perseverance (investments are right only ~53-54% of the time) and learning from experience has turned challenges into wisdom.

title: Its time to learn 7️⃣ : Renaissance Technologies
body:
🎧I will Survive- Gloria Gaynor. 🎧

7️⃣ Jim Simons (Renaissance Technologies)

Jim Simons, the mathematician who founded Renaissance Technologies, is widely regarded as one of the most successful investors ever. His flagship Medallion Fund delivered extraordinary returns—around 66% annualized before fees (and ~39% net) from 1988 through recent decades—generating over $100 billion in trading profits and far outpacing legends like Warren Buffett or George Soros

We reviewed his worst mistake here

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bjpw/when-will-i-learn-7

Now , here  are some of the main things Ken Griffin got right in investing, 
1.  Simons approached investing like code-breaking or pattern recognition in physics/math. By focusing on data-driven signals (not company stories or economic narratives), Renaissance found edges others missed.

2.  A core rule: once a model was live, no human interference.

3.  Simons built teams of mathematicians, physicists, computer scientists, and statisticians (PhDs from non-finance fields).

4.  Renaissance amassed enormous historical and alternative datasets, then used advanced math/stats (e.g., early machine learning like kernel methods, non-linear models, hidden Markov models) to identify small, repeating anomalies.

5.  Instead of big directional bets, they exploited tiny mispricings or relationships (e.g., statistical arbitrage, mean reversion, pairs trading) across thousands of trades daily. High volume + leverage + low costs turned small probabilities into huge compounded gains.

6.  Simons fostered an environment where everyone shared ideas freely—no silos.

7.  No single model dominated; an evolving ensemble adapted to changing markets. They stayed market-neutral where possible (low correlation to broader indices), diversified across assets/classes, and constantly innovated to avoid decay in edges.

8.  Medallion Fund capped size (~$10B) to preserve edges—avoiding the dilution that hurts many funds as they grow.

9. “We don’t start with models. We start with data. We don’t have any preconceived notions.”

10.  Simons emphasized doing something new (“don’t run with the pack”), surrounding yourself with smarter people, being guided by “beauty” in elegant solutions, and sticking with worthwhile pursuits despite setbacks.

6️⃣ Carl Icahn (Icahn Enterprises) 

Carl Icahn is a  legendary activist investor who , pioneered modern shareholder activism. Starting as a “corporate raider” in the 1970s–80s, he evolved into one of the most feared and successful activists, with a long-term track record often cited as among the best (e.g., ~31% annualized returns since 1968 in some analyses, far outpacing benchmarks, and billions in personal gains from campaigns).

We reviewed his worst mistake here

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bju4/when-will-i-learn-6

Now, here  are some of the main things Carl Icahn   got right in investing,  1. 
Icahn mainstreamed taking large stakes in underperforming companies and using influence (proxy fights, board seats, public pressure) to unlock value.

2. 
His core philosophy: “Buy something when no one wants it.” He focused on deeply undervalued assets. He entered when sentiment was negative and exited with big gains after catalysts.

3. 
Icahn made big, asymmetric wagers on his best ideas rather than diversifying broadly. Winners often far outweighed losers (e.g., average winner ~+87%, losers ~-49% in some portfolios), turning a few home runs (like Netflix) into massive compounded returns.


4.  
He identified undervalued assets with fixable problems. He  unlocked hidden value

5.   He accumulated significant stakes (often 5–10%+) gave him real power to negotiate, launch proxy battles, or join boards. 


6.   Icahn waited for resolutions, enduring volatility or opposition, which allowed value creation—contrasting short-term traders. His track record shows strong compounding from perseverance.

7.  Icahn excelled at public pressure, open letters, media battles, and direct talks with CEOs/boards. This often led to concessions (e.g., higher buyout prices in Dell fights, spin-offs at eBay/PayPal, or increased offers), even if full control wasn’t achieved.

8.  He repeatedly pushed for stock buybacks, dividends, or asset sales to return cash directly—arguing overpaid execs and hoarded capital destroy value. Iconic wins include Apple’s expanded buyback program (post-2013 pressure) and various spinoffs.

9.   Icahn rigorously evaluated businesses, concluding favorable ratios in out-of-favor names (e.g., Netflix at lows, Herbalife amid short attacks).

10. Through Icahn Enterprises (IEP), he created a holding company structure for long-term activism. This enabled repeated successes and impressive long-term returns.

title: In the Doghouse:  Madam 8 guide to getting out
body:
A 10-12 min read

🎧 Heard it all before - Sunshine Anderson 🎧

(For Freeballer and all the other 🍆’s out there -💋)


Ladies, We all know the type.
Confident. 
Brash. 
Swinging it around like the room belongs to him.
Thinks he can do no wrong. 
Thinks he is the reason the world keeps spinning.
And for a while… it works.

Until it doesn’t.
Because inevitably

Gasp. Shock. Awe. Surprise.

He says the wrong thing. 
Or Does the wrong thing.
To the wrong person. 
In the wrong place. 
At the absolute worst possible time.

And now?
Now he’s in the doghouse.

Sleeping on the couch. 
Phone blowing up. 
Reddit threads. X posts. Discord . IG on blast. 

“Should we forgive him?” 

“Is this fixable?”

The question isn’t what did he do

It’s “Can we recover?

Oh and before you ask,AfterHour 

Im talking about the president, Donald J. Trump

And his public relationship with the stock market. 👌

💚
Do you need Andy Cohen for a recap? 

The S&P 500 has slid to its lowest levels of 2026.  By slide, we mean It has dipped below key long-term supports like the 200-day moving average

We’re talking about pullback that erased early-year gains and then some, with the index hovering around the 6,500–6,600 range after hitting highs near 7,000 earlier. 

Nasdaq and Dow have followed suit, posting multi-week declines amid broader weakness. 

This is , not panic. Its a sustained distribution phase with lower highs, failed rallies, and fewer stocks participating in any upside. 

💚Let’s be honest about how he got here

Like most men relegated to the doghouse. 
It wasn’t one mistake. 

Not a casual comment about an ex
This was a stack. A pattern. A buildup.

They have been meeting for lunch ever since he said he deleted the number.

The market didn’t just “dip.”
It broke structure.

Oh so now you want details 

Well What had happened was- 

First off 

💚👀 He hasn’t bought the ring when he said he would.

Tariffs weakened or at least removed temporarily. 
￼
Don’t act like you forgot  the Supreme Court struck down broad emergency tariffs in February. This has forced a wind-down of the policy and refunds potentially in the hundreds of billions. 

Like them or not .

Tariffs were a key pillar in trade policy .  

Yes President Trump tried saving face when he pivoted to alternatives like Section 122 (10–15% global tariffs, time-limited) and leaned on Section 232/301 for targeted ones (steel, autos, etc.). 

But uncertainty is a relationship killer.  

The legal fights, refunds, potential expansions hits forward earnings. United States pricing power took a hit while foreign imports stayed competitive longer than expected. 

Profits Margins were squeezed. 
Less profit . 
Less market nookie


💚👀Well aint that some shit. 

U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran starting late February escalated into broader retaliation.

Ugh Yes 

Now here come the messy in-laws.

What was supposed to be a quick “pop in” turned into a full-blown fight.

Im sure Trump thought it would be fast.

It wasn’t.
Now the mother-in-law who said your eggs  were runny at breakfast … is redecorating the spare bedroom. 


💚👀Throughout all this arguing- the result is  messed up plumbing. 

Strait of Hormuz disruptions triggered the biggest oil supply shock on record. 

Oil is  climbing aggressively . 

WTI and Brent are the two biggest benchmarks  for crude oil prices worldwide. Both are high-quality light, sweet crude oils: Easy to refine. Everyone wants it.

That makes them desirable compared to heavier, “sour” crudes that cost more to turn into usable products.

Brent surged past $110–$119 , up 30–50%+ from pre-conflict levels. WTI hitting near $100+.   

Do you remember I told you why  $NVDA will  show her bottom .  

Its would  be because of oil price. 

Every $10 move strangles operating margin for companies.  Companies feel the squeeze. in multiple sectors: industrials, transportation/logistics, airlines, and AI/data centers. And you will see this in their falling stock prices.


💚👀Oh and Bae -  all this fighting in the house is making our Utility bills go up 

Rates are staying higher for longer, with the 10-year Treasury yield sitting around 4.15% to 4.39%.  At those levels, stocks have to deliver much stronger returns just to make the risk worth it.

High-growth names like tech and AI get hit the hardest because their profits are expected far in the future. When yields rise, those future profits are worth less today. That’s why the Nasdaq and growth stocks struggle when rates move up—it’s not couples chemistry, it’s math.

For things to stabilize, yields need to come down and hold somewhere closer to the 3.8% to 4.0% range


💚👀Don’t go running to your sister’s place for a break, because he caused problems there too.

Bonds are now competing harder with stocks. Companies borrow money based on Treasury rates plus a little extra. 

When the 10-year yield goes up, corporate borrowing costs go up too, even if risk stays the same.

That means it’s more expensive to build new factories, expand data centers, or invest in growth. Refinancing old debt becomes painful. As a result, earnings growth slows, future expectations get cut, and stock prices adjust lower.

When rates rise, bonds start paying more, which makes them more attractive than stocks. At the same time, companies feel the pressure. 

Borrowing costs increase, expansion slows down, and debt becomes heavier to carry.
In the end, earnings drop—and stocks follow.


💚👀If that’s not enough, the  kitchen remodeler needs another $20K. 

Suddenly, money feels tight.

Liquidity has shifted. 

From 2022 through late 2025, the Fed was pulling money out of the system by letting bonds expire without replacing them. This reduced bank reserves and drained about $2.4 trillion to fight inflation. That process officially ended in December 2025, with the Fed’s balance sheet stabilizing around $6.6–$6.7 trillion.

Now, instead of draining, the Fed is doing small support moves. They are buying short-term Treasury bills, about $40 billion a month, just to keep enough cash in the system. It’s not real stimulus, just maintenance to keep things steady.
There’s also the reverse repo facility, which used to act like a parking lot for extra cash. At its peak, over $2.5 trillion sat there. Now, in 2026, it’s basically empty.

When that parking lot was full, there was plenty of extra money that could have gone into stocks. Now that it’s drained, that backup support is gone.

So today, there’s less free cash in the system. 
Dip buying is weaker, fewer buyers step in, and when volatility hits, rallies don’t last like they used to.


💚👀And of course , the kids are fighting . 

Congress is stuck in gridlock, and policy keeps getting delayed. With midterm elections coming up, everything becomes more political and less productive.

That means there’s no strong fiscal push to help growth, no clear direction for businesses, and no fast response to rising risks. Companies are left waiting, investors are left guessing, and the market hates both.

When nothing moves forward, uncertainty builds. And when uncertainty builds, investors demand a higher return to take on risk. Who can blame them for taking profits . There will be more sellers than buyers when the kids are fighting in the backseat.

💚This is how we got here 

And here’s what the market relationship starts showing strain. 

While  everyone watching:
Lower highs. 
Weak bounces. 
Failed breakouts. Bad breadth (tech/mega-caps masking broader weakness).
That’s not market panic.
That’s distribution.

So now what ?


💚 How DOES he get out of the doghouse?

Not flowers. 
Not counseling . 
Not more false promises .

Mechanics. Policy. Execution. 
And timing before midterms turn this into a referendum

💅Women like action not lip service.

1.  You said a ring- now make it happen: Reinstate tariffs

This isn’t just “bring tariffs back.” There are real lanes to do it, and some are already in play.

One option is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which targets unfair trade practices, mainly focused on China. It’s led by the U.S. Trade Representative and can be done through executive action, so it doesn’t need Congress. That makes it the fastest and most reliable way to apply targeted tariffs.


Another route is Section 232, which allows tariffs for national security reasons. This has already been used for industries like steel, semiconductors, energy, and autos, so it’s been tested and holds up legally.


A third option is bipartisan legislation tied to supply chains, semiconductors, rare earth materials, and AI hardware. This path takes longer, but it’s more durable and less likely to be challenged in court.

If done right, tariffs can restore domestic pricing power, signal that trade leverage is still intact, and help bring strength back to industrial and materials sectors.

Right now, the market sees that leverage as weakened because of court rulings and refund risks. 

To get back in good standing, he has to prove there will be a ring.

2.  You may not be able to fix your mother-in-law, but you gotta fix the plumbing .  

Ooo. Sensitive subject here: ED. 
Energy diplomacy

For the house to work, but he  will have to fix the plumbing.

This is math, not politics. Oil above $100 is hurting the entire market. 

The solution starts with using the Strategic Petroleum Reserve through well-timed releases to calm price spikes, something that has worked before. 

It also means speeding up domestic production with faster permits, drilling incentives, and tax support for refining. 

At the same time, quiet diplomatic pressure with OPEC and allies can help stabilize output without creating more headlines. The goal is simple: bring WTI and Brent back into a stable $80–$90 range. 

When energy stabilizes, margins stabilize, earnings estimates stop getting cut, and the bleeding slows.

3 .You’re gonna have to find cash from somewhere to pay the remodeler. 

Its not just for $GLD diggers. 

Liquidity  makes the panties wet.   

Markets don’t need fireworks, they need flow. That can come from targeted fiscal spending in areas like infrastructure, defense, and domestic energy, which are more likely to pass even in a divided government. 

Treasury can shift toward issuing more short-term bills to take pressure off long-term rates. Banks can be given regulatory relief to encourage lending, and the Fed can signal flexibility without rushing into rate cuts. When liquidity improves, more stocks participate, credit markets tighten up, and equities find a floor. That’s what turns weak rallies into real



4. Play Nice.- Yes you heard me


 Yes its big.  
We have seen it . 
We have stroked it.
It’s not weakness.  

This  is about getting something done. It doesn’t have to be a grand slam, just a base hit the market can understand. 

That could be a supply chain bill focused on semiconductors and critical minerals, energy permitting reform, or defense spending tied to domestic manufacturing. These moves reduce uncertainty, show that government can still function, and give analysts real numbers to work with. 

Right now, models are breaking because there’s nothing solid to plug in.

5 . No more fighting in public.

 When parents fight,  children fight.   
If its sex twice a day then lets agree on it and make it happen 

Markets hate chaos more than they hate bad news. There needs to be one clear, consistent message around inflation, energy, trade policy, and realistic growth expectations. It has to be simple, repeatable, and steady. 

No surprises. When messaging stabilizes, volatility comes down, and when volatility drops, valuations can start to recover.


6. Love is an action verb… and Ladies love a checklist


👉S&P 500
    Reclaim the 50-day moving average
    Then reclaim the 200-day moving average
    Hold above both (no fake breakouts)

👉Volatility (VIX)
    Needs to drop back below 20
    Stay compressed (no sudden spikes)
   
👉Breadth (participation)
    Advance/Decline line must turn up sharply
    More stocks joining the move, not just a few leaders
    % of stocks above 50-day needs to rise from ~20% (very weak)
    % above 200-day needs to improve from ~45%
   Net new highs must turn positive

👉 Leadership rotation
 Move away from just mega caps (Mag 7 dominance)
  Strength spreads to:
        Small caps (Russell 2000)
        Mid caps
        Value stocks
        Cyclicals (industrials, materials, financials, energy)
        Defensives (utilities, staples)
    Equal-weight S&P (RSP) starts outperforming cap-weighted S&P
    “The many” start leading, not just “the few”
👉 Energy (Oil)
    WTI / Brent stabilize in the $80–$90 range
    No more sharp upward spikes
👉 Rates (10-year Treasury)
    Ease back toward ~3.8%–4.0%
    Stay stable (not jumping higher)


🛑Uh uh. We get the last word 

Its not one
It’s a stack of problems that signals a dealbreaker .

Right now, the market doesn’t feel secure.
Not because there is hate 
But because it doesn’t know what he’s going to do next, and the risks (oil shock, tariff limbo, geopolitics) keep adding up.

Uncertainty?
That’s the ultimate turn-off.
So if he wants out of the doghouse 

We  don’t need flowers. 
We dont  need apologies.
We need action
Because the market isn’t asking: “Do you love me?”
It’s asking:
“Can you lead under real pressure… when it actually counts?”

title: Its time to learn 5️⃣ :
body:
🎧 levitating- Dua Lipa 🎧

5️⃣ Ray Dalio (Bridgewater Associates) 
an American billionaire investor and hedge fund pioneer. He founded Bridgewater Associates in 1975 from his two-bedroom Manhattan apartment, growing it into the world’s largest hedge fund (managing around $92 billion as of recent reports). Starting investing at age 12 (tripling money on Northeast Airlines stock), he earned a BS in finance from Long Island University and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

We reviewed his worst mistake here👇

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bjAT/when-will-i-learn-5

Now, here  are some of the main things Ray Dalio   got right in investing,  1
Dalio and Bridgewater foresaw the housing bubble and excessive leverage risks as early as 2007. In 2008, while stocks plunged ~37% and most hedge funds lost ~19–20%, Bridgewater’s flagship Pure Alpha fund gained ~9% by going long bonds, gold, and other safe havens.

2
Developed in the 1990s (initially for his family trusts, later scaled), the All Weather strategy balances assets.  (allocating roughly 30% stocks, 40% long-term bonds, 15% intermediate bonds, 7.5% gold, and 7.5% commodities . It became a benchmark for “weathering any storm” and influenced the broader industry.

3
Since 1991, Bridgewater’s Pure Alpha strategy (systematic macro with ~12% volatility target) has annualized high single digits, with only four losing years over 30+ years. It excels in bear markets (e.g., strong in 2008 and reportedly +32% in early 2022 volatility) by using hundreds of uncorrelated signals for balanced bets.

4
His accurate calls on fixed income, currencies, and overlays earned awards (e.g., World’s Best Money Manager in 2002 for 16.3% returns). This built the foundation for scaling to $100B+ AUM by the 2010s and proving systematic fundamental macro as a repeatable edge.

5
Dalio has long advocated gold as a diversifier against debt/money-printing risks (recommending 10–15% allocation). Bridgewater’s heavy gold/commodity exposure (plus family office bets on gold ETFs) paid off in inflationary periods, while recent portfolio shifts (e.g., large S&P 500 ETF increases in 2025 alongside AI/semiconductor plays like Nvidia/Oracle) show adaptive macro positioning.

title: Its time to learn 3️⃣ :
body:
🎧 AOK - Tai Verdes 🎧

3️⃣ Peter Lynch (Fidelity Magellan Fund )
American investor, mutual fund manager, author, and philanthropist.


We reviewed his worst mistake here

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bjKX/when-will-i-learn-3

Now, here  are some of the main things Peter Lynch   got right in investing,  1.  Peter Lynch transformed the Fidelity Magellan Fund through his disciplined, common-sense approach of “invest in what you know,” relentless bottom-up research, and focus on companies with strong earnings growth and reasonable valuations (popularizing the PEG ratio). 

 Under his leadership, the fund’s assets exploded from $18 million to over $14 billion, attracting more than a million shareholders.

2️⃣Benjamin Graham (Graham-Newman Corporation)

Benjamin Graham ( widely regarded as the “Father of Value Investing.”)  in 1936 co-founded the Graham-Newman Corporation with Jerome Newman. 

He taught at Columbia Business School (where Warren Buffett was his student) and authored the investing classics Security Analysis (1934, with David Dodd) and The Intelligent Investor (1949).


We reviewed his worst mistake here

https://afterhour.com/883Ismygovtname/bjR8/when-will-i-learn-2


Now, here  is what he did right. 

Graham succeeded by buying undervalued securities with a strong margin of safety.  This meant purchasing assets well below their intrinsic value to limit downside risk while preserving capital. 

 Graham’s wins included activist-style plays like 

1. pressuring Northern Pipeline to distribute excess assets for large dividends, 

2. purchase of 50% of GEICO for $712,500—a low-cost direct-to-consumer insurer trading below intrinsic value. The GEICO stake (later distributed to investors) exploded in value; one early investor’s small holding grew to over $1.6 million by 1972. 

3. Graham emphasized rigorous fundamental analysis, financial strength (strong balance sheets, consistent earnings, dividends), and avoided speculation—principles that protected capital 

He influenced generations, including Buffett. He  retired from active management in 1956 at the top of his game.

Buffett succeeded by evolving former teacher, Benjamin Graham’s value investing. He bought high-quality businesses with durable competitive advantages (“economic moats”) at fair or attractive prices.

He then held  them for the long term to harness the power of compounding. 

Key successes include the massive long-term gains from holdings like Coca-Cola, American Express, Apple, and GEICO. He had a  disciplined approach—focusing on understandable businesses with strong management, avoiding speculation, and maintaining a large cash reserve for opportunistic buys. 

Under his leadership since 1965, Berkshire Hathaway delivered a compounded annual return of approximately 19.9% through 2024 (versus ~10.4% for the S&P 500), resulting in a staggering total return exceeding 5 million percent and creating hundreds of billions in shareholder value. A true 🐐

title: 😈DCA is Foreplay :
body:
🎧Drunk in Love - Beyonce 🎧


“We woke up in the kitchen saying how the hell did this shit happen oh baby”


*A 5 minute read*

Dollar-Cost Averaging Is Foreplay
The Slow Burn That Builds Real Wealth
Listen.
I get it. I GET IT.


There is absolutely nothing sexy about the term dollar-cost averaging.

“Dollar?”
Who wants a dollar? I want millions.

“Cost?”
Now it sounds transactional. Like I need to list what I bring to the table.

“Averaging” 
When it comes to the bedroom 
No one is swiping for averages 


Because what you actually want is orgasmic returns 
 the kind that build, expand, and surprise you over time 

But guess what?

Dollar cost averaging might be the most seductive strategy in investing.

🫦What Dollar-Cost Averaging Actually Is

Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) simply means investing a fixed amount of money on a regular schedule.
Bring your lunch to work one day
Instead
$5 a week 
$100 every paycheck. $300 on the first of the month.
 Rain or shine. Red or green.

You don’t wait for the “perfect” time. You don’t panic when markets dip. You don’t FOMO when they surge.

You show up.
You tell her she’s beautiful
You send her a check-in text

Again. And again. And again.
Until that portfolio explodes with profit 

🫦Why This Works (And Why It Feels So Calm)

When prices are high, your fixed dollars buy fewer shares.
 When prices are low, your fixed dollars buy more shares.

Over time, your average cost smooths out.

You stop trying to be brilliant. You start being consistent.

Volatility stops feeling like red flags and starts feeling like opportunity.

DCA Is Foreplay
Lump-sum investing is the “all at once” move.
It’s what most people think about when they think about investing.

Quick entry
Large exposure. High emotional stakes.
Big finish

Yeah Sometimes that works. but often,  it leaves you stunned.
Nowhere close to the goal

DCA?
That’s foreplay.
It builds  It lowers anxiety. It creates comfort and trust with the process.

For women, foreplayv isn’t optional. It’s where safety is built. It’s where anticipation develops. It’s what transforms an experience from mechanical to meaningful.

DCA does the same thing for investors.
You ease into exposure. You let your nervous system adapt. You stay engaged instead of overwhelmed.
And over time, that slow burn compounds.

🫦Don’t Even Start Physical
You start mental.
Set the picture and what do you want the future to look like.

Before you invest a dollar, ask:

Do I want exposure to a broad index? $SPY. A specific sector? $ QQQ. Growth? Dividends? Both? $ SCHD.

If I earn dividends, will I reinvest them? Let them compound? Use them to DCA elsewhere into another Mag 7 stock.

Paint the picture first.
Then automate it.
Set it.
Forget it. Let it run.

🫦Why This Matters for Small Accounts
If you’re building with:
A paycheck. A side hustle.
You probably don’t have a giant stack of cash waiting to deploy.

Your real choice isn’t lump sum vs. DCA.

It’s DCA vs. Sitting in cash waiting for “the right time.”


And no one can perfectly time the market

For small accounts especially, the biggest risk isn’t slightly lower returns.

It’s never starting. Or quitting during a downturn.
DCA protects the habit.
And habits build wealth.


🫦The Math Reality (Without the Ego)
Historically, lump-sum investing beats DCA about 70–75% of the time because markets trend upward over long periods.


BUT

that assumes you already have the full lump sum ready.

Most don’t.
If you’re broke, you can STILL be a good market lover. 
How can that be?

Most people are investing gradually as they earn.
And in that real-world DCA wins by default 


It keeps you in the game.
Women like familiarity . Less regret. Consistency. 


🫦The Quiet Millionaire Strategy

John “Jack” Bogle built Vanguard on this principle.  He  used low cost index funds + automatic investing.

Warren Buffett has repeatedly said most people should regularly invest in a low-cost S&P 500 fund rather than try to pick winners.


Peter Lynch encouraged steady investing in what you understand rather than market timing.

Even macro legends like Ray Dalio emphasize systematic, rules-based investing over emotional decision-making.

Look around you on AfterHour

There are Quiet millionaires who auto-invested $200–$400 per month for 20–30 years.

No headlines. Just compounding.


The real wealth stories aren’t the traders who timed one perfect entry.

They’re the quiet investors who auto-invested $200–$400 per month for 20–30 years and let compounding do its thing.

Slow. Predictable. Relentless.

🫦The Chandeliers
At first, DCA feels boring.
Then steady. Then reassuring.
And then one day — you look up and your portfolio is doing something different.
The profits  are pressing upward

Momentum builds. Dividends compound. Growth stacks on growth.
Panties are wet and she is returning calls 
People ask how you did it.


No  gambling 
No guessing  Never panicked
You were consistently.
And now?
Guess who is swinging from the chandeliers.

🫦Snuggle time

Dollar-cost averaging isn’t explosive on day one.
It’s patient. Disciplined. Intentional.
It turns volatility into advantage. It removes procrastination. It builds wealth without requiring genius-level timing.

It puts haters to sleep 
Start small. Automate it. Keep going.
Because in investing 
just like in romance
the slow burn often delivers the most unforgettable finish.

And yes.
That’s pretty sexy.

🎧“The last thing I remember is our beautiful bodies grinding up in that club”🎧

Yesterday we tackled similarities in the varied landscape between the United States and Iran

How about the people in America? We celebrate Independence Day from British rule . Every July 4 Americans gather together with fireworks to honor American pride. We all know it as Independence Day. Iran has their similar celebration for their independence in 1979.

The 1979 Iranian Revolution (also called the Islamic Revolution) was a major popular uprising in Iran that overthrew the monarchy of Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and replaced it with the Islamic Republic of Iran. It occurred primarily between 1978 and early 1979, culminating on February 11, 1979 (known as “Victory Day” or 22 Bahman in the Iranian calendar).

The 1979 Revolution transformed Iran from a secular monarchy aligned with the West into a theocratic republic emphasizing Shia Islamic governance, independence from foreign powers, and export of the revolution. It reshaped Middle East geopolitics, contributed to the rise of political Islam globally, and created enduring tensions with the United States and Sunni Arab states. 

Domestically, it brought social and cultural changes (e.g., mandatory hijab, Islamic legal system) alongside ongoing debates over its legacy—economic challenges, repression of dissent, and debates about pre- vs. post-revolution life persist today.

🎧 What have you done for me lately:  - Janet 🎧

If you think YOUR gas is expensive

Recall from yesterday NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket (used for the Artemis program):

The Per-flight operating cost is Approximately $4 billion per mission (including the Orion spacecraft and ground systems). Just the hardware alone runs $2.5 billion+ per launch.

Now let’s compare it to the EV equivalent in space — SpaceX’s Falcon 9, the most common commercial rocket today:

The Customer launch price: $67–$74 million per reusable flight to low Earth orbit.  SpaceX’s internal/marginal cost: As low as $15–20 million per launch, thanks to first-stage reusability (boosters now fly 20+ times).

The Fuel cost only $150,000–$250,000 for a full load of liquid oxygen (LOX) and RP-1 kerosene — less than 0.3–1% of the total launch price.

Starship/Super Heavy (SpaceX’s next-gen system, still in testing) has Fuel cost: Around $800,000–$1 million per full stack (liquid methane + LOX). 

Full operational launches aren’t even routine yet, but the numbers are already impressive.

So in comparison Reusability has slashed the cost per kilogram to orbit from ~$54,000/kg in the Shuttle era down to ~$2,500–$3,000/kg on Falcon 9 — a massive drop!

That’s still pricey for most of us, but Elon is finding a way to save a lot of money.

If you ever get to watch a launch in person, you might just wanna snap a picture of this historical moment unfolding. Don’t forget to bring your camera… and thank NASA 

Yep 

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory worked on miniaturized, low-power, high-quality imaging sensors for spacecraft cameras to capture scientific data in space. 

That complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) active-pixel sensor technology helped enable compact, energy-efficient cameras. It directly influenced modern smartphone cameras, webcams, medical imaging devices, and digital photography .

title: Planting Seeds :  🙄Why bother with small Portfolios
body:
🎧 The Seed (2.0) – The Roots 🎧

There’s a belief that you can’t succeed in the market without a financial advisor.

Not true.

You can invest on your own. The tools are there. The information is everywhere. What matters isn’t having an advisor but a process.

An advisor’s real value isn’t secret stock picks, It’s discipline.

Think of a small portfolio like a seed.

In  elementary school, kids are sent home with a sunflower seed bag and a paper towel  They  watch what happens. Not every seed becomes turns into a towering sequoia.

But that’s not the point.

The point is learning how growth works.

Small portfolios do the same thing. They teach you patience, timing, and care. They show you what happens when you nurture something consistently. And while small investors aren’t children, smart adults understand that big results often come from starting small.

Where people go wrong is simple. They skip the advisor and also skip the plan.  
Newbies please Don’t Chase headlines. 
Don’t buy high because it’s exciting. 
Don’t sell low because it’s scary.

Your money needs somewhere to grow. It should be working for you. It could be in an interest-bearing account. It could be in a stock with upside. You’re not limited. You can always adjust, always sell, always reposition. 

The key is that your money is planted, not sitting idle.

Consider letting someone manage the large  portion while you learn and observe and learn with a small amount . Thats what I do. 

You don’t need an advisor to start.
Just plant the seed. stay consistent with watering. 

Of course, this is not financial advice :)

Now lets get dirty

title: I don’t hate Christopher: Zeng He

🎧 Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies – Fiona Sit   🎧

“1492, Columbus sailed the ocean blue.” 

what’s rarely taught is that he wasn’t alone

Other explorers were charting vast waters and building global connections prior to Christopher Columbus.  Lets take  Zheng He (Chinese, 1371–1433): an admiral of the Ming Dynasty who led seven major voyages between 1405 and 1433 . He had massive fleets with hundreds of ships and tens of thousands of crew. 

His expeditions reached Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East, and East Africa (modern-day Kenya and Somalia.  A display of Chinas powerful trade networks and naval capability.

Having a new portfolio is  like  being an explorer stepping onto what feels like untouched ground, it’s easy to believe you’re the first to begin this journey.

Although you are not first , it doesn’t make your path any less meaningful. Building a portfolio isn’t about being first; it’s about being prepared. With a plan in hand, you’re not wandering. You are navigating. 

If you’re really scared .  I say 90% in an index fund and 10% of the cash as experimental. That 10% of the portfolio you can use to buy 100 shares of a stock you like, run covered calls, learn to sell and buy options, and practice.

My first year I tried all kinds of things.

Dont end up with a shipwrecked portfolio 

Newbies :

With careful planning, and the right guidance, your portfolio can go as far as the Polynesians did.

Btw 

Did you know about the Polynesian sailors?  . The Master navigators from Hawaii . They used stars, ocean swells, wind patterns, birds, and oral knowledge (no compasses or maps).

They settled Hawaii (from Marquesas or Society Islands) around 1000–1200 CE.

By Reaching New Zealand (Aotearoa), Easter Island (Rapa Nui), and nearly every habitable island in Polynesia they traveled incredible distances. Hawaii from Marquesas is  about 2,400–2,500 miles of open ocean. Tahiti to Hawaii ~2,200 miles. Round-trip voyages and settlement across the “Polynesian Triangle” spanned thousands of miles over centuries. 

They  effectively “discovered” and colonized the largest ocean on Earth long before Europeans

 Abu Bakr II . , the  west African Ruler (or predecessor to Mansa Musa) who reportedly abdicated to explore the Atlantic Ocean.

 he sent a large fleet (hundreds of ships) westward across the Atlantic around 1311–1312 to find what lay on “the other side.”

He equipped a second, larger expedition (up to 2,000 ships) after the first didn’t return and sailed with it himself. He never returned.

This is a historical debate. I will admit.  There is no definitive proof of reaching the Americas. If real, Abu Bakr II could have crossed thousands of miles (the Atlantic is ~3,000+ miles wide at equatorial latitudes). 

. It would show West African capability for large-scale ocean voyages using currents and boats. 

Why is it debated at all? 

Indigenous accounts recorded by Christopher Columbus and Bartolomé de las Casas: Natives of Hispaniola (Caribbean) reportedly told Columbus that “black-skinned people” had arrived from the south/southeast in boats, trading with gold-tipped spears made of a metal called guanín (or guanin). Chemical analysis of similar alloys showed a composition (roughly 18 parts gold, 6 silver, 8 copper) matching West African metallurgy, not local sources.

body:
🎧 Merrily  we all Roll Along  (The Warner Bros Fanfare) -Sydney Symphony Orchestra 🎧


Happy Father’s Day to all the fathers of the past, present, and future.

Last year I did a week-long presentation on cartoon fathers to show my appreciation.

This year  I haven’t been on AfterHour as much. 
Instead, I’m focused on building my following on X.  But Daddies of all types are still on my mind. 

I’ll be tying together themes of the market, White History Month

Ironically, My father was never a fan of some of the images I and siblings saw on television. As a young child, I thought they were innocent, fun, and playful. Now that I’m older, I better understand the discomfort he must have felt. 

At the same time, they still makes me laugh. So over on X, I’ll be reviewing some of the most notorious racist cartoon images and the branding, marketing, and business decisions behind them.

As for the portfolio, I’m playing it safe.

The plan remains simple: stack shares.

It would be nice to reach 1,000 shares of $SOFI before it’s all said and done. 

You may see me jump back into SpaceX for a swing trade later this week, but otherwise I’m sitting tight and protecting capital.

My advice?

Be grateful for the lemon.

Do what you can to make the best of this current political situation. Stack your shares. Because when the sugar finally arrives, all you'll have left to do is make lemonade.

$BWEN, $FERMI, and $OKLO are probably at the top of my watchlist right now. I’m also keeping an eye on $HPE, $SMCI, $NVTS, and $SYM.  Not really looking for any new tickers right now.  

Outside of investing, I’m having a wonderful summer with the kids. Hitting the gym. Rearranging my life to create more free time. Putting dating on hold yet again. Building out projects on Substack.
